title: An Open Heart for Christ and His Church
speaker: Unknown Speaker
summary: Paul addresses the Corinthians' spiritual decline, not from false doctrine or external persecution, but from hearts grown cold toward Christ and faithful ministry. The greatest obstacle to spiritual faithfulness is often misplaced affections rather than lack of knowledge. Paul calls believers to enlarge their hearts through the gospel, ordinary spiritual disciplines, and loving both Christ and His church.

outline.title: The Greatest Danger Facing a Church: A Gradual Cooling of the Heart
subpoints: The danger is not primarily false doctrine, persecution, or moral compromise, but hearts that grow cold toward Christ
A congregation may continue to meet, sing, and pray while its love for Christ quietly diminishes
The problem is fundamentally one of affections, not intellect or knowledge

outline.title: A Faithful Minister Removes Unnecessary Obstacles to the Gospel
subpoints: Paul demonstrates through his ministry that he has not placed stumbling blocks before the Corinthians
Paul emphasizes endurance and suffering as evidence of his care for God's people
Christian ministry is advanced through God's truth and power, not through manipulation or worldly techniques

outline.title: The Corinthians' Problem Is Their Own Hearts, Not Paul's Ministry
subpoints: Paul's heart is open, but the Corinthians are restricted by their own affections
Their hearts have become spiritually narrow, closed off, and attracted to flattering teachers
Spiritual decline begins long before people bend biblical truth; hearts wander first

outline.title: The Cure for Spiritual Decline: An Enlarged Heart
subpoints: Paul appeals for the restoration of covenantal affection and wholehearted love
A narrow heart produces resentment, suspicion, bitterness, and pride
An enlarged heart produces love, generosity, forgiveness, patience, and unity
Only the Holy Spirit can truly enlarge the human heart through the ordinary means of grace

outline.title: Four Practical Applications for Enlarging Our Hearts
subpoints: Examine our affections: What excites us? What disappoints us? What do we treasure most?
Be aware of a shrinking heart: Bitterness, envy, unforgiveness, worldliness, and pride all shrink the heart
Love Christ's people: We cannot love Christ while despising His body, the church
Respond to Christ's open heart with our own enlarged hearts filled with love

tags.tag: Love for Christ and the Church

transcript:
## Scripture Reading

> "We give no offense in anything that our ministry may not be blamed, but in all things we commend ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in tribulations, in needs, in distresses, in stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labors, in sleeplessness, in fastings, by purity, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Spirit, by sincere love, by the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armor of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, by honor and dishonor, by evil report and good report, as deceivers and yet true, as unknown and yet well known, as dying and behold, we live, as chastened and yet not killed, as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing and yet possessing all things. O Corinthians, we have spoken openly to you, our heart is wide open, you are not restricted by us, but you are restricted by your own affections. Now, in return for the same, I speak as to children, you also be open." (2 Corinthians 6:3-13)

## The Greatest Danger Facing a Church

During the winter of the Valley Forge encampment, the greatest threat to the Continental Army was not just the cold and hunger. The greatest threat was morale. Soldiers lacked shoes, clothing, and food. Many were wondering whether the cause was worth the sacrifices they were going through. Yet George Washington remained among them. He was one of the few commissioned officers that stayed in camp with the everyday soldiers, sharing their hardships rather than abandoning them. His steadfast presence rekindled their commitment, and by spring the army emerged with renewed resolve.

Paul presents something similar but greater. He did not abandon the Corinthians when they criticized him. He endured hardship and misunderstanding, persecution and suffering for their spiritual good. Yet despite his steadfast love for them, many had grown cold toward him.

Their greatest danger in Corinth, and I believe this is the greatest danger in church in general, was not external opposition but hearts that no longer appreciated faithful ministry. In the same way as Paul, Christ has never abandoned His people. He remains the faithful shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep. When our affections grow cold, when our affections move us away from Christ, the answer is not to find a different shepherd but to return to the one whose love has never changed.

### The Danger of a Gradually Cooling Heart

One of the greatest dangers facing a church is not primarily false doctrine, nor persecution from outside, nor even moral compromise. The greatest danger facing a church is a gradual cooling of the heart. To quote the great theologian Keith Green, "Lord, relight the fire that once burnt bright and clear." How many of us are in need of praying that prayer?

Those of us who were converted later in life can remember when the Lord brought us to Christ. Sometimes we crave that zeal that was present in those early years—a zeal for the gospel, a zeal for Christ, a zeal to see people saved. A gradual cooling heart is a dangerous thing.

A congregation may continue to meet, may continue to sing and pray, and may continue even to affirm sound doctrine while its love for Christ, its love for His ministers, its love for one another quietly diminishes. Nothing drastic, nothing quick, but just day-to-day living. The temperature keeps dropping and we don't notice. If we don't do something about it, eventually we're going to freeze to death with cold hearts toward the Lord Jesus Christ.

This is exactly what Paul addresses in this passage. Throughout this letter, he has defended his apostolic ministry—not because his personal reputation was at stake, but because the gospel of Jesus Christ was at stake. He doesn't care whether people like him personally, but he must defend himself when the gospel is at stake and when it's dangerous for the people.

### The Real Problem: Misplaced Affections

Here the Corinthians' rejection of him revealed something about their own hearts. They revealed that they were drifting away from the gospel itself. Paul concludes this section with an astonishing diagnosis. He does not blame their intellect for the problem. He does not say they lack evidence of the truths of the gospel. He does not say they need more arguments, though he presents arguments throughout the letter. He says that their problem is their hearts.

One wise theologian said that he stared his enemies in the eyes, and the enemy was us. We tend to be the biggest enemy of the gospel, the biggest enemy of ourselves in the gospel, because we let our hearts cool down from the love of Christ and the love of God in Jesus Christ.

Here the issue is not merely what they think. The issue is what they love. How often is that the issue with us? We think the right things. We have the right knowledge. But that knowledge does not warm our hearts and drive us to love the Lord Jesus Christ and through Him love those that belong to Him.

### The Main Point of Application

The greatest obstacle to spiritual faithfulness is often not lack of knowledge but misplaced affections. God causes people to enlarge their hearts toward Christ and His church. In medicine, a large heart is a bad thing, but in faith, the bigger your heart, the closer to Christ you are.

## A Faithful Minister Removes Unnecessary Obstacles

We see here in verses 3 through 10 that a faithful minister removes unnecessary obstacles to the gospel. The Corinthians are accusing Paul of not being a faithful minister. Paul says, "Look, I have not put an obstacle before you. I have not set up barriers. I have not been a stumbling block to you by immorality, by wrong attitudes, by wrong doctrine."

He can honestly say that he has not given offense to the Corinthians. His ministry cannot be blamed for the Corinthians' attitude toward Christ. What a special thing to be able to say and have it be true! To be able to stand before God and His people and say, "I have never set a stumbling block before you that kept you from seeing Jesus."

As Christians, can we say that we have not put a stumbling block in the way of other people? As parents, can we say that we have not put a stumbling block in the way of Christ before our children? As husband and wife, can we say that we have not put a stumbling block before our spouses in the way of Christ? May God give us grace to be there or to get there.

Paul knows that ministers are not perfect, but they must never intentionally place stumbling blocks before God's people.

### The Ministry of Endurance

Notice how often Paul emphasizes endurance as he defends his ministry in verses 4 through 10. He says that he experienced afflictions, necessities, distresses, stripes, imprisonments, tumults, labors, sleeplessness, and hunger. He's simply refuting the idea that the Corinthians are expressing—that he didn't care for them. "Would the things I've done for you show that I don't care or that I care for you?" This is hardly the resume of the false apostles in Corinth.

The false apostles have promoted comfort and their own glory. Paul displayed the cross of Christ. Paul's theology of ministry was one of suffering, one of the cross, not one of glory. He was willing to do that for God's people.

Brothers and sisters, are we willing to suffer for each other? Is our view of life one that emphasizes the cross or glory? Are we after the glory of God—which should be only His—or are we willing to suffer as our Savior suffered for us on behalf of one another?

### The Spiritual Resources of a Faithful Minister

Paul then lists the spiritual resources that sustained him as a minister to the Corinthians. The first one he lists is purity. "Do you want to know that I haven't been a stumbling block before you?" Paul says. "I behave toward you in godliness." How important it is that we go that way.

Purity, knowledge, longsuffering, kindness, the Holy Spirit, sincere love, the word of truth, and the power of God were his tools. Paul demonstrates to us that Christian ministry is not advanced through manipulation or worldly techniques but through God's truth and God's power.

Then he describes a series of paradoxes of the Christian faith. As Christians, we are dishonored and yet honored, sorrowful and yet always rejoicing, poor yet making many rich, possessing nothing and yet possessing everything. This is the power of Christ Himself.

The servant of Christ measures success differently than the world. People say that Paul was dishonored, yet he was honored by Christ Himself. People say that he was always sorrowing, yet he was rejoicing in Christ. People say that he was poor, yet he had the riches of Christ at his disposal.

### A Different Standard of Success

Brothers and sisters, the standards by which we evaluate our ministry are not worldly standards. It's not popularity. It's not entertainment. It's not charisma. It's not financial success. It's not the number of people in pews. It's not how many friends we can have at church.

The true measure that we must use is: Is Christ preached faithfully? Is that what you're looking for in the church? Is the word of God proclaimed? Is holiness pursued? Is suffering endured with joy?

In a few Sundays, we're going to be communicating to you a particular disciplinary matter. Why? Because God calls us to pursue holiness. Pray for your elders and your congregation as we try to faithfully follow our Lord, even when it hurts, even when we have to declare someone to be outside of the Church of God, outside of the assurance of God's love for them.

## The Corinthians' Problem Is Their Own Hearts

When we get to verse 11, we see that the Corinthians' problem was not Paul's heart but their own. Paul says, "O Corinthians, we have spoken openly to you. Our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted by your own affections. Now in return for the same, I speak as to children. You also be open."

Here we see the passage changing dramatically. Paul moves from defending himself to saying, "Look, the problem is not with how I minister to you. The problem is with your own heart." Paul moves from defending his ministry to pleading for their hearts. These are the tender words of a pastor who loves his sheep.

Paul did not hold anything back. His speech has been open. His heart has been open. He has loved them sacrificially despite their criticism.

### The Saddest Statement

And then comes one of the saddest statements in the New Testament in verse 12: "You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted by your own affections."

The problem is not Paul. The problem is not the gospel. The problem is not the church. The problem is their affections. The Greek word for "restricted" speaks of being crimped or confined. Their hearts have become spiritually narrow. They have closed themselves off. They have become suspicious of faithful correction. They have become attracted to teachers who flatter them. Their loves have become disordered.

This is often where spiritual decline begins. Long before people bend biblical truth, their hearts have already wandered off.

### Our Affections Direct Our Lives

Our affections direct our lives. What we love directs our lives. Our Savior said in Matthew 6:21, "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." What you value, what's important to you, is what's going to direct your life. If that is anything less than Christ, your North Star is going to be off course, and you're going to end up in the wrong place.

We inevitably move toward what we love. The Corinthians still attended church. They still professed Christ. But their hearts were drifting elsewhere.

Brothers and sisters, they are no different than us. We tend to read the Bible and think, "Oh, those bad people back then. I can't believe they would do that." And yet what Paul has given us here is actually a look into the human heart, not just the Corinthian heart.

How much of our marriages, how much of our marriage troubles, are there because of our closed heart to the Lord? How much of our relational problems are there because of our closed heart to love? How much of our problems are there because we treasure something other than Christ and His love for us?

## The Cure: An Enlarged Heart

In verse 13, Paul gives us the cure for spiritual decline. The cure is an enlarged heart. Again, as far as health goes, you don't want an enlarged heart. But as far as serving Christ, that's the best thing for you.

Paul says, "Now in return for the same, I speak as to children. You also be open." Paul concludes with a fatherly appeal. It is important that we realize that Paul is not asking for personal admiration. He's asking for the restoration of covenantal affection. "I have loved you. Would you love me as well?" That's what Paul is asking.

This language echoes the covenant relationship God repeatedly sought with Israel. God continually calls His people not just to obedience but to wholehearted, wide love.

### The Effects of a Narrow Heart Versus an Enlarged Heart

Brothers and sisters, a narrow heart produces resentment. A narrow heart produces suspicion. A narrow heart produces bitterness. A narrow heart produces isolation. A narrow heart produces pride.

An enlarged heart, on the other hand, produces love, generosity, forgiveness, patience, and unity.

### How the Gospel Enlarges Our Hearts

The gospel is what enlarges our hearts. The gospel enlarges hearts because Christ first loved us and gave Himself for us. At the end of the day, though, only the Holy Spirit can truly enlarge the human heart, because the natural heart is curved inwardly in itself. If you're an unbeliever, the Bible says that number one in your life is yourself. Sin shrinks our loves, but grace expands.

John Calvin made the famous statement that the human heart is a factory of idols. When idols occupy the heart, our love for Christ necessarily diminishes. The answer is not simply greater discipline. The answer is renewed affection for Christ. As our hearts are captivated by His beauty, lesser loves lose their power.

### The Ordinary Means of Grace

This happens by the ordinary things that God has appointed: reading the Bible, praying, being in the Lord's house, fellowship with God's people, participating in the sacraments. That's how God and Christ grow more beautiful to us.

I often find people who are losing their affection for Christ. The first thing they do is stop these practices. And then they wonder why Christ is not precious to them. They stop praying. They isolate themselves from the church. And they wonder why Christ is not so beautiful.

Because brothers and sisters, do you want to see Christ? Look to the person to your left. Look to the person to your right. If you look at a believer in Jesus Christ, that's the best way to see Christ—by looking at His body, His church.

## How Shall We Then Live? Four Final Applications

### First, Examine Our Affections

Let's look into our hearts and examine what it is that we love. What excites us the most? What excites us more than anything? Is it the praise of people? Is it other people serving us? What is the beauty of God in the face of Christ? What occupies our imaginations? What are we thinking about all the time? Are we thinking about what people have done to us, how they've hurt us, how we can get back at them? Or is the gospel of Jesus Christ consuming our imaginations?

What disappoints us most when it's taken away? Our honor? Our glory? Our reputation? What is it that we can't afford to lose? Those answers to these questions often reveal the true condition of our heart.

### Second, Be Aware of a Shrinking Heart

Bitterness shrinks the heart. Envy shrinks the heart. Unforgiveness shrinks the heart. Worldliness shrinks the heart. Pride shrinks the heart.

Ask the Lord to enlarge your heart through His word. It's a simple, ordinary means that God has given us: word, prayer, sacrament.

Life is not lived in the big moments. Life is lived in the little moments—the toilet seat lid left up, the toothpaste tube without the cap on, the door left unclosed. I've seen marriages survive adultery and not survive those little mundane 10,000 moments of life.

God, knowing that, gave us the ordinary, everyday things to enlarge our heart: the reading, especially the preaching of His word; prayer; and our worshiping together and participating in the sacraments.

### Third, Love Christ's People

We want a large heart to love Christ's people. The Corinthians claimed devotion to Christ while distancing themselves from Christ's appointed minister. We cannot love Christ while despising His body.

The love for Christ produces increasing love for the church. If you say, "I love Jesus, but I just don't like His people," you don't love Jesus. One of the first teachers I had to fire, a school principal, said that she loved teaching. She just didn't like the kids. If there were no kids, working at the school would be amazing. Does she really love teaching? It's the same with the church. If you don't love the body of Christ, you don't love Christ. It's that simple.

## Paul's Final Appeal

Paul's final appeal is deeply personal. He says, "My heart is open to you. Will yours be open to me?" This is ultimately the voice of Christ Himself.

Christ has opened His heart to sinners. He has withheld nothing from them. He gave His body. He shed His blood. He bore God's wrath. He rose again. Now He calls His people to respond—not merely with words or obedience, but with enlarged hearts filled with love. Not just any kind of love, but love for Him and love for His people.

The greatest question this pastor asks is not just, "Do you believe the right things?" Though we must. The greatest question is, "To whom does your heart truly belong?"

May God, by His Spirit, enlarge all of our hearts so that we love Christ above all, cherish His word, embrace His church, and gladly receive every faithful means He has appointed for our growth in grace. May that be true of all of us.
